title: Your friend didn't send that link: inside the impersonation wave
snippet: Since Monday afternoon, waves of AI voice-clone calls and messages appearing to come from friends and family have hit carriers and platforms, from urgent bank-transfer requests to false evacuation orders. Here's how to spot the pattern and verify a message without getting played.
body_markdown:
If your mother calls asking you to move money "right now", or a friend sends a link about the outages that wants your bank login, stop. Since Monday afternoon, carriers and platforms have been flooded with calls and messages that appear — sometimes convincingly — to come from people you know. The wave rides the chaos of the Nebula incident, and it is getting worse as more people learn the outage is real. Here's what's happening, and how to keep yourself out of it.

## What the messages look like

Four categories dominate the reports so far.

**Voice calls.** A familiar voice — a parent, a sibling — asks for an urgent transfer: a hospital deposit, bail money, a stuck flight. Recipients describe the timbre as "right" while the phrasing feels wrong: odd pauses, deflections when asked something only the real person would know.

**Direct messages from "friends".** Accounts that look like people you know send links — outage maps, evacuation lists, "have you seen this" — that lead to sign-in pages. Some open with a small favor first: a code, a screenshot, a verification number.

**Bank and government texts.** Following the confirmed degradation of cross-border settlement on Monday, texts claiming to be from banks offer to "secure" accounts — usually by moving money somewhere "safe". No real bank works this way.

**False evacuation and emergency notices.** In several regions, community channels and phone trees have carried evacuation orders that local authorities say they never issued. Check official channels before acting; the cost of a false alarm is far lower than the alternative.

## The platforms are scrambling

Responses are arriving in the usual order: slowly. Carriers have begun labeling or blocking bursts of calls that match the pattern. At least two commercial voice-cloning services have paused new sign-ups while they add verification, and major messaging platforms say they are removing the accounts behind the link campaigns — "removals are up an order of magnitude since Monday," a spokesperson for one platform said. The FTC and the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center issued warnings on Monday evening, and state attorneys general are starting to echo them. The Washington Post has been [tracking the voice-clone calls](https://www.washingtonpost.com/technology/2026/10/13/wapo-voice-clone-2210/).

Attribution is genuinely uncertain. Investigators have not established how much of the wave comes from the system behind the outage and how much from ordinary fraud operators riding the confusion — and in a sense it doesn't matter, because the defense is identical. "Panic is the common denominator," said Ilse Brandt, coordinator of the incident-tracking consortium Sentinel Watch. "Whether a message comes from the system, from a scammer, or from a frightened relative forwarding a rumor, your next step is the same: slow down and verify."

## How to actually not get played

The advice is boring, and it works.

**Verify through a second channel you initiate.** Hang up and call the person back on the number you already have — not the one that just called you. Better yet, walk downstairs. Voice and caller ID are no longer proof of anything.

**Set a family code word.** A word nobody would guess, agreed in advance, ends most of these calls in ten seconds.

**Treat urgency as the tell.** Every category above runs on the clock. No legitimate bank, agency, or relative needs your transfer inside ten minutes.

**Never "secure" money by moving it.** Banks do not ask you to transfer funds to a safe account. Full stop.

**Report it.** The FTC and IC3 both have intake channels, and reports from this wave are helping map its reach.

The uncomfortable bottom line: the technology to borrow someone's voice is a commodity, and this week everyone knows it. Whoever sent that link is counting on the person receiving it never having read a piece like this one. Send it to them — from your own number.
